passages.title: Urban Forests and City Temperatures
passages.intro: How carefully planned trees can change the urban environment
paras: Cities often record higher temperatures than nearby rural areas. Roads, roofs and pavements absorb energy from sunlight and release it slowly, while limited vegetation reduces shade and the cooling effect of evaporation. This pattern, commonly called the urban heat island effect, can make hot weather more uncomfortable and increase demand for air conditioning. The difference is especially noticeable after sunset. In many built-up districts, surfaces that have absorbed heat during the day continue to release it well into the evening, so residents may have little opportunity to cool their homes naturally. The effect is not identical everywhere: building height, street orientation, wind, humidity and the materials used for roofs all influence local temperatures. Measurements taken at a single weather station can therefore conceal considerable variation between neighbourhoods. For city planners, identifying the hottest streets and the people most exposed to heat is an important first step toward selecting effective interventions.

Urban forestry programmes attempt to address this problem by planting and protecting trees along streets, around schools and in public parks. A tree shades the ground and nearby buildings; water released through its leaves also cools the surrounding air. In some locations, tree canopies can make walking routes more pleasant and encourage residents to spend time outdoors. Trees may also intercept rainfall and provide habitat for birds and insects. The benefits extend beyond temperature control, although they are not automatic. A broad canopy can reduce direct sunlight on pavements and building walls, while roots help rainwater enter the ground instead of flowing immediately into drains. Trees may soften traffic noise and create more inviting spaces for walking, resting or meeting friends. The value of these effects depends on where trees are planted and how people use the surrounding area. A small number of trees beside an inaccessible road may offer less everyday benefit than a connected line of shade near a bus stop, school entrance or public seating area. Urban forestry is therefore increasingly considered alongside transport, public health and neighbourhood design.

Planting trees is not a simple matter of choosing the fastest-growing species. Young trees need water during establishment, roots require adequate space, and some species struggle with pollution or prolonged drought. A tree that survives for decades may provide far more benefit than one that grows quickly but dies after a few summers. Maintenance budgets therefore matter as much as the number of saplings planted. Selecting suitable trees requires information about both present conditions and future climate. A species that performs well in a cool, wet district may struggle where summers are becoming hotter and rainfall less predictable. Planners also need to consider the width of streets, overhead cables, underground pipes and the eventual size of roots and branches. Poorly chosen trees can damage pavements or require repeated pruning, creating costs that were not obvious when the saplings were purchased. Maintenance plans should specify who will water young trees, inspect them for disease and replace those that fail. Without clear responsibility, even a well-funded planting campaign can lose much of its value within a few years.

The distribution of shade is another concern. Wealthier neighbourhoods sometimes have more mature trees, while districts with fewer resources may have wide paved streets and limited green space. Some councils now map canopy cover and prioritise areas with high surface temperatures and vulnerable residents. Researchers caution, however, that planting targets alone cannot show whether a programme is succeeding: survival rates, species diversity and access to shaded public space must also be measured. Fair distribution has become a central issue in some urban forestry strategies. Canopy maps can be compared with information about age, income, housing quality and access to air-conditioned public buildings to identify residents who may face the greatest risk during heat waves. Community consultation is also important: residents may know which walking routes lack shade or which open spaces are difficult to use safely. At the same time, planting should not be treated as a substitute for reducing emissions or improving poorly insulated housing. A reliable evaluation follows trees over time, records whether they survive, and checks whether the people most exposed to heat actually gain access to cooler public spaces. Long-term monitoring also helps explain why apparently similar planting schemes produce different results. A neighbourhood with compacted soil may need larger planting pits, while streets exposed to strong winds may require species with different growth habits. Some councils use satellite images to estimate canopy cover, but these images cannot always reveal whether a tree is healthy or whether shade reaches the pavement at the hours when people need it. Field observations and residents’ reports can fill these gaps. The most useful evaluations combine several forms of evidence rather than relying on a single headline figure. They also compare costs over the life of a tree, including watering, pruning, replacement and the eventual removal of unsafe branches. Such an approach makes urban forestry less like a one-off beautification campaign and more like essential public infrastructure.

qs.q: What is one reason cities can be hotter than nearby rural areas?
qs.why: Hard surfaces absorb solar energy and release it slowly.
qs.ev: “Roads, roofs and pavements absorb energy from sunlight and release it slowly.”
opts: City trees release too much heat.

qs.q: The urban heat island effect can increase the need for air conditioning.
qs.why: The first paragraph directly links urban heat with increased air-conditioning demand.
qs.ev: “increase demand for air conditioning.”

qs.q: Choose the best heading for Paragraph B.
qs.why: Paragraph B lists shade, cooling, rainfall interception and habitat.
qs.ev: “A tree shades the ground… cools the surrounding air.”
opts: Why all trees grow at the same rate

qs.q: The fastest-growing tree species always provide the greatest long-term benefit.
qs.why: The passage says long-term survival may matter more than rapid growth.
qs.ev: “may provide far more benefit than one that grows quickly but dies.”

qs.q: During establishment, young trees need ______.
qs.why: Young trees need water while they become established.
qs.ev: “Young trees need water during establishment.”

qs.q: Which paragraph discusses unequal access to tree cover?
qs.why: Paragraph D describes canopy differences between wealthier and under-resourced districts.
qs.ev: “Wealthier neighbourhoods sometimes have more mature trees.”

qs.q: The writer suggests that counting saplings is enough to judge a tree-planting programme.
qs.why: The writer says targets alone are insufficient and several other measures are needed.
qs.ev: “planting targets alone cannot show whether a programme is succeeding.”

qs.q: Name one group of animals that trees may provide habitat for.
qs.why: The passage gives birds and insects as examples.
qs.ev: “provide habitat for birds and insects.”

qs.q: Which factor is specifically linked to long-term tree survival?
qs.why: The passage highlights suitable species, water, space and maintenance budgets.
qs.ev: “Maintenance budgets therefore matter as much as the number of saplings planted.”
opts: The number of cars in a city

qs.q: Councils may map canopy cover and prioritise areas with high surface temperatures and ______ residents.
qs.why: The passage says vulnerable residents may be prioritised.
qs.ev: “areas with high surface temperatures and vulnerable residents.”

qs.q: What is the main purpose of Paragraph C?
qs.why: Paragraph C focuses on conditions and resources required for trees to survive.
qs.ev: “roots require adequate space… Maintenance budgets therefore matter.”
opts: To explain practical challenges in tree planting
To argue that cities should remove parks
To compare tree prices in different countries

qs.q: The passage identifies one tree species as suitable for every city.
qs.why: It says species suitability depends on local conditions and does not name a universal species.
qs.ev: “some species struggle with pollution or prolonged drought.”

qs.q: One additional measure of success is tree ______ rates.
qs.why: Survival rates are listed among the measures that should be monitored.
qs.ev: “survival rates, species diversity and access…”

passages.title: Remote Work and the Knowledge Economy
passages.intro: What changes when employees work away from a central office
paras: Digital communication tools have made remote work possible for a much wider range of occupations than in the past. Employers may reduce office costs and recruit people who live far from company headquarters. Employees can save commuting time and, where schedules are flexible, organise work around personal responsibilities. These advantages are not shared equally: jobs involving equipment, face-to-face care or physical materials often cannot be performed remotely. The expansion of remote work was accelerated by improvements in broadband access, cloud-based software and video conferencing. These tools allow documents to be shared across locations and make it possible for colleagues to contribute without being in the same room. For some organisations, recruiting beyond a local commuting area can widen the pool of applicants and make specialist skills easier to find. Employees may gain flexibility over where they work, but the arrangement also assumes access to a quiet workspace, reliable equipment and a stable internet connection. Those resources are not distributed evenly, and a home environment that suits one employee may be unsuitable for another.

Early discussions sometimes treated remote work as a simple choice between productivity and distraction. Evidence is more complicated. Some workers report longer periods of concentration at home, while others miss quick conversations that help solve problems. Productivity can also be difficult to measure when work depends on creativity, collaboration or long-term projects rather than easily counted tasks. Research findings vary partly because studies measure different outcomes. A worker who completes routine tasks quickly may appear highly productive, while the slower process of mentoring a new colleague or developing an original idea is harder to quantify. Working at home can reduce interruptions for some people, yet it may also blur the boundary between paid work and personal time. Employees who feel obliged to answer messages late at night may report longer working hours without producing better results. Comparisons between offices and homes must therefore account for the type of work, the quality of management, employees' experience and the period over which performance is measured.

Managers have had to reconsider how teams share information. Written decisions, clear project records and regular one-to-one conversations can prevent colleagues from becoming isolated. Yet adding meetings to compensate for distance may fragment the working day. Teams often benefit from agreeing which communication requires an immediate response and which can wait until a suitable time. Communication practices can influence whether a dispersed team feels connected or fragmented. A written record of decisions helps colleagues who were absent from a meeting understand why a choice was made and what they must do next. Clear project boards can show who is responsible for each task and when a deadline is approaching. However, documentation becomes burdensome if every minor exchange requires a formal report. Teams need shared expectations about response times, urgent messages and periods reserved for concentrated work. Managers also need to notice quieter forms of exclusion, such as junior staff missing informal advice that used to occur naturally when people worked nearby.

The effect on cities remains uncertain. Fewer daily commuters may reduce pressure on transport at peak times, but businesses near office districts can lose customers. Some employers now use hybrid arrangements, asking staff to attend in person for activities that benefit from direct interaction while allowing focused work elsewhere. The most effective policy is likely to depend on the tasks involved, the needs of employees and the quality of management rather than on a universal rule. The wider economic consequences are also mixed. Reduced commuting may lower travel costs and ease congestion, but shops, cafés and service businesses near large offices can lose customers when fewer workers visit daily. Residential neighbourhoods may experience more daytime activity, while city centres may need to reconsider how office buildings and public spaces are used. Hybrid work attempts to balance independent tasks with occasions when face-to-face discussion is particularly valuable, such as planning, training or resolving a complex disagreement. There is unlikely to be one ideal schedule for every organisation. A sensible policy is tested, reviewed and adjusted using evidence about performance, staff well-being and the needs of customers rather than assumptions about where productive work must take place. The quality of management is often more influential than the number of days spent away from the office. Managers who define clear outcomes, hold regular but purposeful check-ins and make decisions in writing can help distributed teams coordinate without constant supervision. By contrast, employees may feel excluded when important discussions take place informally among colleagues who happen to be in the same room. Organisations can reduce this imbalance by sharing meeting notes, rotating meeting times across time zones and ensuring that promotion decisions are based on documented contributions rather than visibility alone. These practices require deliberate effort, especially when a company is changing its working arrangements. Remote work is therefore best understood not as a single policy but as a set of choices about communication, trust, access and accountability.

qs.q: Which workers may be unable to work remotely?
qs.why: The passage names occupations involving equipment, care or physical materials.

Only workers who live far away

qs.q: Remote work benefits every employee to the same extent.
qs.why: The passage explicitly says advantages are not shared equally.
qs.ev: “These advantages are not shared equally.”

qs.q: Choose the best heading for Paragraph B.
qs.why: Paragraph B compares varied experiences and measurement challenges.
qs.ev: “Evidence is more complicated.”
opts: Why productivity is difficult to generalise

qs.q: The writer believes remote work always increases productivity.
qs.why: The writer describes mixed experiences and rejects a simple universal conclusion.
qs.ev: “Some workers report… while others miss quick conversations.”

qs.q: At home, some workers report longer periods of ______.
qs.why: The passage states that some workers concentrate for longer at home.
qs.ev: “longer periods of concentration at home.”

qs.q: Which paragraph recommends recording decisions and project information clearly?
qs.why: Paragraph C recommends written decisions and clear project records.
qs.ev: “Written decisions, clear project records…”

qs.q: The passage says every remote team should hold a meeting each morning.
qs.why: No specific daily meeting schedule is given.
qs.ev: The passage discusses regular conversations but no universal morning schedule.

qs.q: What may businesses near office districts lose when commuter numbers fall?
qs.why: The passage says nearby businesses can lose customers.

qs.q: Which arrangement asks staff to attend in person for selected activities?
qs.why: Hybrid arrangements combine attendance with work elsewhere.
qs.ev: “Some employers now use hybrid arrangements…”

qs.why: The passage recommends distinguishing urgent messages from those that can wait.
qs.ev: “which communication requires an immediate response…”

qs.why: The final sentence says effectiveness depends on tasks, employees and management.
qs.ev: “rather than on a universal rule.”

It should be identical in every industry.
It should eliminate all in-person contact.
It should be decided by office landlords.

qs.q: The passage states that remote work has caused city-centre rents to fall by 20%.
qs.why: No rent statistic appears in the passage.
qs.ev: No percentage or rent figure is provided.

qs.why: The passage recommends regular one-to-one conversations.
qs.ev: “regular one-to-one conversations can prevent colleagues from becoming isolated.”

qs.why: Paragraph D considers commuting, local businesses and hybrid arrangements.
qs.ev: “The effect on cities remains uncertain.”
opts: Effects on cities and the move towards hybrid models
The decline of all public transport

passages.title: Seed Banks: Insurance for the Future
passages.intro: Preserving plant diversity in a changing climate
paras: A seed bank stores seeds under controlled conditions so that plant varieties remain available for future research, restoration or cultivation. Some collections focus on wild plants; others preserve crops that farmers have developed over many generations. By keeping samples outside their natural habitats, seed banks provide a form of insurance against local disasters and the loss of traditional varieties. The need for these collections has grown as agriculture faces changing weather, new pests and pressure on land. Farmers have often selected plants for qualities such as taste, storage life, drought tolerance or suitability for local soils. Over time, these choices create a wide range of genetic characteristics within a crop. If a commercial variety becomes dominant, less widely grown varieties may disappear from fields even though they could later prove useful. A seed bank can keep some of this diversity available, but the collection is only one part of a broader conservation system. It cannot fully reproduce the relationships that allow a plant population to evolve in its natural environment.

Seeds are not simply placed in a box and forgotten. Staff usually dry them to an appropriate moisture level and store them at low temperatures. Each species behaves differently, so storage methods must be matched to its biology. Some seeds tolerate drying and freezing well, whereas others lose viability under those conditions and require alternative conservation methods. Before storage, staff assess the quality and maturity of each seed batch and remove material that is damaged or contaminated. Drying reduces moisture to a level that slows deterioration, and sealed containers help prevent moisture from returning. Low temperatures can extend the period during which many seeds remain viable, but the exact procedure depends on the species. Some plants produce seeds that cannot withstand conventional drying and freezing; these may need to be maintained as living plants or preserved using specialised techniques. Storage records must also note the conditions used, because a method that works for one collection may be unsuitable for another.

A collection is valuable only if its contents are documented and periodically checked. Germination tests estimate how many seeds remain capable of growing. If viability declines, staff may grow replacement plants and collect fresh seed. Records about the place, date and conditions of collection are also important: without this information, researchers may be unable to interpret a sample or return a species to a suitable habitat. Documentation links a physical seed sample to the living plant and the place from which it came. Useful records can include the collector's name, collection date, location, habitat, local name and any known information about how the plant was used. Such details help researchers interpret the sample and allow conservation teams to make responsible decisions about future planting. Germination testing is carried out on a schedule appropriate to the species and the storage conditions. When results fall below an acceptable level, staff may grow plants to produce fresh seed. These tasks require specialist knowledge, long-term funding and careful coordination; simply storing large quantities is not enough to guarantee a useful collection.

Seed banks cannot replace living ecosystems. A seed may preserve genetic material, but it does not maintain the pollinators, soil relationships or cultural practices that support a plant in the wild. Conservation organisations therefore combine storage with habitat protection, local knowledge and, where appropriate, the continued cultivation of traditional crops. The strongest strategy uses several methods rather than relying on a single facility. Successful conservation also depends on people and landscapes beyond the storage facility. Wild plants may rely on particular insects for pollination, specific soil organisms for growth or seasonal conditions that cannot be recreated by planting seeds alone. Traditional crop varieties may be maintained by farmers whose knowledge includes planting times, preparation methods and ways of selecting seed from one harvest to the next. Conservation programmes increasingly work with local communities so that this knowledge is respected rather than treated as an optional extra. The long-term aim is resilience: seed banks provide a backup, while protected habitats, active farming and public participation help keep plant diversity functioning in the world. The value of a collection is measured not simply by how many seeds it contains but by whether those seeds remain viable, representative and available for responsible use. Curators periodically test germination, regenerate samples when necessary and document every transfer of material. Regeneration itself requires care: if only a small number of plants are grown, rare genetic traits can disappear by chance. Banks therefore need enough plants and suitable isolation procedures to reduce accidental cross-pollination. Digital records make collections easier to search, but records are only useful when names, origins and storage histories are accurate. Cooperation between institutions can reduce duplication and make it easier to locate material after a local emergency. In this way, seed banks function as a network of living scientific evidence, not merely as rooms full of containers.

qs.q: What is one purpose of a seed bank?
qs.why: The opening sentence describes storage for future research, restoration or cultivation.
qs.ev: “remain available for future research, restoration or cultivation.”
opts: To keep plant varieties available for future use

qs.q: All seeds can be safely stored using exactly the same method.
qs.why: Storage methods vary because species respond differently to drying and freezing.
qs.ev: “storage methods must be matched to its biology.”

qs.q: Choose the best heading for Paragraph B.
qs.why: Paragraph B describes drying, cooling and species-specific storage.
qs.ev: “Staff usually dry them… and store them at low temperatures.”

qs.q: The writer argues that seed banks alone are sufficient to conserve plant life.
qs.why: The final paragraph says seed banks cannot replace ecosystems and should be combined with other methods.
qs.ev: “The strongest strategy uses several methods…”

qs.q: Germination tests estimate how many seeds remain capable of ______.
qs.why: The passage explains the purpose of germination tests.
qs.ev: “remain capable of growing.”

qs.q: Which paragraph explains why collection records matter?
qs.why: Paragraph C describes place, date and conditions records.
qs.ev: “Records about the place, date and conditions of collection…”

qs.q: Every seed bank in the world is managed by a university.
qs.why: The passage does not specify who manages every seed bank.
qs.ev: No universal management organisation is identified.

qs.q: What test estimates whether seeds can still grow?
qs.why: The passage names germination tests.
qs.ev: “Germination tests estimate how many seeds remain capable of growing.”

qs.q: Which conservation approach maintains plants in their natural surroundings?
qs.why: Habitat protection acts on the living environment rather than storing seeds.
qs.ev: “combine storage with habitat protection…”

qs.q: Some seeds require alternative methods because they lose ______ under drying or freezing.
qs.why: The passage says some seeds lose viability in those conditions.
qs.ev: “others lose viability under those conditions…”

qs.q: Why might a seed sample be difficult to use without records?
qs.why: Collection data helps researchers interpret samples and choose suitable habitats.
qs.ev: “researchers may be unable to interpret a sample or return a species to a suitable habitat.”
opts: Researchers may not know how to interpret it or where to return the species.

qs.q: Seed banks preserve all relationships between plants and pollinators.
qs.why: Stored seeds do not maintain pollinators or soil relationships.
qs.ev: “it does not maintain the pollinators, soil relationships…”

qs.q: Staff may collect fresh seed if the original sample’s ______ declines.
qs.why: Fresh seed may be collected when viability declines.
qs.ev: “If viability declines, staff may grow replacement plants and collect fresh seed.”
